meta.note: Exam-style written questions. Chapter 2 has 4 MCQs (Stage 2) and 11 long-form exercises here.

questions.question:
Write word equations and then balanced equations for the reaction taking place when –
(a) dilute sulphuric acid reacts with zinc granules.
(b) dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium ribbon.
(c) dilute sulphuric acid reacts with aluminium powder.
(d) dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with iron filings.
questions.model_answer:
(a) Zinc + Sulphuric acid → Zinc sulphate + Hydrogen
**Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)**

(b) Magnesium + Hydrochloric acid → Magnesium chloride + Hydrogen
**Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)**

(c) Aluminium + Sulphuric acid → Aluminium sulphate + Hydrogen
**2Al(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)**

(d) Iron + Hydrochloric acid → Iron(II) chloride + Hydrogen
**Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)**

questions.question: Compounds such as alcohols and glucose also contain hydrogen but are not categorised as acids. Describe an Activity to prove it.
hints: Set up bulb circuit with dilute HCl and with glucose/ethanol solutions.
Acids ionise in water to give H⁺; glucose/ethanol do not.
questions.model_answer:
**Activity:** Connect a bulb circuit with dilute **HCl**, **glucose solution**, and **ethanol solution** separately.

The bulb **glows brightly** with dilute HCl (H⁺ ions conduct electricity) but **does not glow** (or glows very dimly) with glucose or ethanol solutions because they **do not produce H⁺ ions** in water despite containing hydrogen.

Hence they are **not acids**.
marking_points: Glucose or ethanol does not ionise to H⁺
common_mistakes: Saying all hydrogen-containing compounds are acids

questions.question: Why does distilled water not conduct electricity, whereas rain water does?
hints: Distilled water has almost no ions.
Rain water dissolves CO₂ and other gases forming acids.
questions.model_answer:
**Distilled water** is almost pure H₂O with **very few ions**, so it is a **poor conductor**.

**Rain water** dissolves **CO₂** and other gases from the atmosphere forming **carbonic acid** and other electrolytes, producing **ions** that make it conduct electricity.
common_mistakes: No mention of dissolved gases in rain water

questions.question: Why does dry HCl gas not show acidic behaviour in the absence of water?
hints: HCl ionises only in presence of water.
Dry gas has no free ions.
questions.model_answer: **Dry HCl gas** does not show acidic behaviour because **acids produce H⁺ (hydronium) ions in aqueous solution**. Without water, HCl molecules do **not ionise**, so no H⁺ ions are available to show acidic properties (no effect on dry litmus, no conductivity).
marking_points: H⁺ ions needed for acidic behaviour
Water required for ionisation of HCl
Dry HCl has no free H⁺
common_mistakes: Confusing with dry litmus test only

questions.question:
Five solutions A, B, C, D and E when tested with universal indicator showed pH as 4, 1, 11, 7 and 9, respectively. Which solution is
(a) neutral?
(b) strongly alkaline?
(c) strongly acidic?
(d) weakly acidic?
(e) weakly alkaline?
Arrange the pH in increasing order of hydrogen-ion concentration.
hints: Lower pH = more H⁺ = more acidic.
Higher pH = less H⁺ = more basic.
questions.model_answer:
(a) **Neutral:** D (pH 7)
(b) **Strongly alkaline:** C (pH 11)
(c) **Strongly acidic:** B (pH 1)
(d) **Weakly acidic:** A (pH 4)
(e) **Weakly alkaline:** E (pH 9)

**Increasing H⁺ concentration** (decreasing pH): **C(11) < E(9) < D(7) < A(4) < B(1)** i.e. **11, 9, 7, 4, 1** for pH values from least to most H⁺.
marking_points: Correct pH order for H⁺ concentration

questions.question: Equal lengths of magnesium ribbons are taken in test tubes A and B. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is added to test tube A, while acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is added to test tube B. Amount and concentration taken for both the acids are same. In which test tube will the fizzing occur more vigorously and why?
hints: HCl fully ionises; acetic acid partially.
questions.model_answer:
Fizzing occurs more vigorously in **test tube A (HCl)**.

**HCl** is a **strong acid** — it produces **more H⁺ ions** at the same concentration.

**Acetic acid** is a **weak acid** — it ionises only partially, so fewer H⁺ ions are available; reaction with Mg is **slower** and fizzing is less vigorous.
marking_points: HCl is strong acid / more H⁺
Acetic acid is weak / partial ionisation

questions.question: Fresh milk has a pH of 6. How do you think the pH will change as it turns into curd? Explain your answer.
hints: Curd formation involves lactic acid bacteria.
questions.model_answer:
As milk turns into **curd**, its **pH decreases** (becomes **less than 6**, more acidic).

Lactic acid bacteria convert lactose to **lactic acid**, increasing H⁺ concentration and lowering pH.

questions.question:
A milkman adds a very small amount of baking soda to fresh milk.
(a) Why does he shift the pH of the fresh milk from 6 to slightly alkaline?
(b) Why does this milk take a long time to set as curd?
hints: Baking soda is NaHCO₃ — basic salt.
Higher pH slows bacterial acid production.
questions.model_answer:
(a) **Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate)** is mildly **basic**; it **neutralises** slight acidity and shifts pH from 6 to **slightly alkaline**.

(b) Curd forms when lactic acid bacteria produce acid, lowering pH. **Alkaline milk** retards this process, so the milk **takes longer to set** as curd.
marking_points: (a) baking soda is basic / raises pH
(b) alkaline medium slows curdling / acid production
common_mistakes: Saying baking soda makes milk acidic

questions.question: Plaster of Paris should be stored in a moisture-proof container. Explain why?
hints: Reacts with water to form gypsum.
questions.model_answer:
**Plaster of Paris** (calcium sulphate hemihydrate) **reacts with moisture/water** to form **gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O)**, a hard mass that **cannot be used** for moulding.

Hence it must be stored in a **moisture-proof container**.

questions.question: What is a neutralisation reaction? Give two examples.
questions.model_answer:
A **neutralisation reaction** is the reaction between an **acid and a base** to form **salt and water**.

**H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)**

Examples:
1. **NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)**
2. **Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CaSO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)**
common_mistakes: Products as hydrogen and oxygen gas

questions.question: Give two important uses of washing soda and baking soda.
questions.model_answer:
**Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O):**
• Used in **glass, soap, and paper industries**.
• Used for **cleaning** and **removing permanent hardness** of water.

**Baking soda (NaHCO₃):**
• Used as **antacid** (neutralises stomach acid).
• Used in **baking** (releases CO₂ with mild acid) and **fire extinguishers**.
marking_points: At least two uses of washing soda
At least two uses of baking soda
